notes.citation: Propertius, Elegies, book 3, the last elegy (3.25, lines 5–6)
notes.original: Properce au iij. liure, Elegie dernier.
notes.gloss: The couplet quoted at the head of the next annotation.

english.html: This made great evidence of the good faith of the said de Rols, and that she never had the will to stray from her true consort and husband, nor in any way to violate the faith she owed him, although she had in fact carnally cohabited with the same du Tilh. For if a woman converses with another, thinking him to be her husband, so long as she is ignorant of it she cannot be called an adulteress, but only from the hour when she knows it and says no word of it <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>. Which the said de Rols did not do; but, on the contrary, from the moment she began to discover and to perceive the prodigious fraud in which the said du Tilh — cunning, subtle, malicious, and the most dissembling lecher that ever was — had so finely lulled her, she pursued him virtuously, sparing neither her goods nor her pains.

notes.citation: Gratian, Decretum, c. Si virgo, at "C. 33 q. 2" as printed — the chapter stands in the modern division at C. 34 qq. 1–2 c. 5; the same citation as annot-075 {r}
notes.original: c ſi virgo. xxxiij. q. ij.
notes.gloss: The woman who, deceived, lies with a man she believes to be her husband commits no adultery while the error lasts; she becomes an adulteress only if, learning the truth, she continues and says nothing — the rule Coras states.

english.html: Whereupon it will not be out of place to recount the countenance of the newcomer, who, having shed tears at the confrontation and at the meeting with his sisters, nevertheless at the great weeping and extreme lamentations of the said de Rols never showed a single sign of grief or sadness: but on the contrary, with an austere and fierce countenance, and scarcely deigning to look at her, said to her: Put aside these tears, by which I cannot, nor ought I to, be moved.
